title: The Maids
wpTitle: The Maids reviews round-up at the Donmar Warehouse in London directed by Kip Williams

ratings.excerpt: Leaves you dizzy … Australian director Kip Williams turns Genet’s psychodrama into a dazzling digital-age headrush … You could say that this take on Jean Genet’s 1947 psychodrama of theatrical, erotic and murderous fantasy was A Lot. You might even think it was A Bit Much. But babe, you’d be wrong. It’s way, way more excessive than that – and all the more thrilling for it. … As in Dorian Gray, the piece unfolds on video and mocked-up social media as well as on stage. The pace is frenetic, the colours vivid, and the overall effect a headrush that leaves you dizzy, dazzled and – I suspect deliberately – faintly nauseous. … With lip-licking relish and wild, reckless abandonment, all three women take it turns to flip the bitch switch, chattering inanely in text-speak and wellness woo woo... If you're prepared to surrender, it's a wild ride … This adaptation of Jean Genet’s play by Kip Williams makes use of phones to project the fantasy world of two sisters wishing to murder a terrible mistress but the true power is in the performances … In Australian auteur Kip Williams’s version, adapted and updated to a world of Instagram followers and filters, and running a high-octane 100 minutes, I finally got it. … This is a hectic, shouty psychodrama which barrages the audience with emotion and imagery. … Williams draws powerful and intricately precise performances from a magnetic Lydia Wilson and relative newcomers Phia (House of the Dragon) Saban and Yerin (Bridgerton) Ha. … It is, frankly, a lot. Dorian Gray’s Kip Williams dazzles again with feverish fantasy … There are superb performances in this screen-saturated staging of Jean Genet’s play, updated for the influencer age … Screens feature just as extravagantly in this three-hander that sweeps you into its turbulence at relentless speed. … Written and directed by Williams, this new version is a brash, eye-popping take on Jean Genet’s 1947 drama … Williams gives a modern meaning to the play through the technology itself: influencer image-making and online celebrity culture are critiqued. … The pumping music and Insta imagery wobbling in the hands of characters as they film themselves gives the play its hallucinatory, unravelling quality. Hotly-tipped Aussie director Kip Williams’s live video-centric take on the Jean Genet classic is gloriously lurid … ... The Maids is his first original UK production. And the question begged is: are all Kip Williams’s shows ‘like that’, in a visual sense? The answer would seem to be ‘basically, yes’. … Visually it’s loud, garish and kind of basic. Which is a good thing! ... live video is one of the more dominant means of communication on the planet. The fact Williams uses it in a somewhat trashy, teenagery way is fun, reflective of our times, and offers a great way into modernising Genet’s play. … As well as looking incredible, Williams’s root and branch modern update of Genet’s text is very funny. The maids tear eye-wateringly vicious strips off each other … It’s exhilarating, hilarious,

Like being locked in a cupboard with Katie Price … Kip Williams’s manic revival of Jean Genet’s psychodrama is packed with clever effects but does nothing to solve the play’s mysteries … The set is the winner in this manic update of Jean Genet’s psychodrama, a Gallic exercise in demented role-playing, now given a modern influencer gloss by that ultra-fashionable Australian director and adaptor Kip Williams. … Williams’s rewrite throws in flurries of references to today’s online world and its jaded hangers-on. … In the opening barrage of dialogue — both actresses deserve maximum credit for maintaining such a breathless flow of words throughout the evening — they are half-concealed behind a silky curtain. … But with so little variation in pacing, the exchanges begin to grind us down. Jean Genet’s drama becomes a vicious satire of the TikTok age … The Australian director Kip Williams brings a queasy contemporaneity to the suffocating 1947 play … Political metaphor, erotic fantasy, quasi-religious ceremony, it’s still a troubling, provocative watch. Williams’ sugar-rush of a production retools it as a vicious satire of the TikTok age and its distortions of reality. … Genet’s fascination with performance and identity here re-emerges to embrace the current weird credo that if you are not on show, you somehow don’t exist. … Genet’s depiction of brittle celebrity, economic inequality and marginalised individuals is made disconcertingly timely by Williams. What unfolds is a tightly wound, high-decibel psychodrama, full of raised voices and rapid-fire emotion. … Rosanna Vize’s hyper-realised set and costumes do much to anchor the production. … The production is, without doubt, a feast of bells and whistles – technically immaculate, visually audacious, and conceptually dense – but that polish sometimes comes at the expense of intimacy. … Performances are suitably adept. Saban and Wilson hurl themselves into the roles with frenzied commitment … The piece becomes a reflection on how social media turns status into performance, friendship into currency and self-worth into statistics. … Where Dorian Gray succeeded, this Maids sometimes falters. Jean Genet’s absurdist shocker gets a glib update for the TikTok era … Australian director Kip Williams radically reimagines the 1947 satire – to limited effect … Its titular skivvies serve a twentysomething billionaire mistress who puffs pineapple vapes, drapes herself in haute couture finery and cossets a labubu. While these delulu women inhabit a plausible contemporary setting, however, there's something infuriatingly glib and apolitical about this update. … ... the everpresent projections of smartphone displays don't do much to enhance this story. Genet’s classic The Maids is reduced to Snapchat and screeching … Kip Williams’s screen-fuelled staging of the French playwright’s psychodrama is borderline unwatchable … ... alas: even a crack cast that includes Lydia Wilson can’t prevent this souped-up take on the self-delusions of Instagram culture from feeling as though you’ve descended into TikTok’s seventh circle of hell. … Genet’s melodrama embraces excess. Correspondingly, so does Williams’s production. … On one level, the play is well suited to the Williams treatment. Its hall-of-mirrors structure … There is a difference between interrogating these ideas and merely embracing them. Absolutely unwatchable 'I felt like I was being assaulted in my seat' … The Donmar Warehouse's update of Jean Genet's 1947 psychodrama about murderous maids is one of the worst nights I've ever spent in the theatre. … For 100 interminable minutes that felt far, far longer, three actors on stage screamed at each other, at full speed, non-stop, barely taking a breath. It's exhausting. … And let me be clear. All three actresses on stage do a Titanic job remembering and wrangling the ridiculously machine gun torrent of text and the ever-shifting, always manic and never profound, moods and tones. … Yes, there are interesting themes about our addiction to social media, our addiction to unreality...
